title: Inside Beauty Banking: Top Women Dealmakers Discuss Career Paths, Trends, and the Current Dealscape
text:
How four leading women in beauty investment banking are shaping the industry through landmark deals and breaking barriers.
Pelaez has over 18 years of experience advising consumer and retail clients globally, with a particular focus on the beauty and wellness sector. Prior to Ardea, she was a director at RBC Capital Markets in New York where she led beauty and wellness.
Radic has been making a name for herself in the beauty banking world, working on some of the buzziest initial public offerings and deals. Notable transactions include the Nutrafol sale to Unilever, Ouai to P&G, Chantecaille to Beiersdorf and Charlotte Tilbury to Puig. Leading JPMorgan’s charge into beauty, Zhang has been tapped by some of today’s hottest founders to explore deal options. Notable transactions: Waldencast’s acquisition of Milk Makeup and Obagi, Olaplex’s IPO.
I attended NYU Stern School of Business for my undergraduate degree, and studied finance and management, so it was a very natural segue. I started my career at JPMorgan as a summer intern back in 2011, and I’ve stayed with the firm for my career. I studied at Brandeis University, a liberal arts college, so definitely did not study finance, but focused on math and econ so there was a through line.
I networked with alumni and friends trying to find a way in because I had loans to pay, and thought that it could be an interesting first step out of school. I made my way to Bank of America Merrill Lynch where I started. I was there for two years and then moved to Jefferies, where I’ve been for the last 13 years. : Similar to Fei-Fei — NYU undergrad Stern.
I was a double finance and accounting major with a minor in French. I also interned at JPMorgan. I was a huge Francophile, so instead of joining JPMorgan, I joined BNP Paribas because they promised me a secondment in Paris. After the first year in the M&A team in New York, I went to Paris on a three-year contract, which was wonderful because I did a lot of things across continental Europe.
For personal reasons I came back after a year and spent a couple years in the leverage finance team, and then joined RBC. I went to Brown University, and I was an American history major. I joined the merchandising program at Bloomingdale’s as an assistant buyer in fashion accessories, and became a senior assistant buyer in trend jewelry.
After two years, I was telling my friend I didn’t know what I wanted to do, and she’s like, “Well, I’m going to business school, and so somebody needs to take my role. ” She was an equity research analyst at Lazard, covering media. I said, “That’s great, but I know nothing about finance” and she said, “Come to my apartment every day for the next week,” and she gave me a crash course.
I did not get the job, but later I got a call from the retail and apparel analyst there who said “come in and be my associate. ” I realized that I liked the companies, but I didn’t know which way the stocks were going to go. So I went to business school at Columbia Business School.
Then a little boutique firm called Financo found my name in the résumé book and they’re like, ah, someone who knows retail and finance, and so they called me in for an interview, and I went in on a whim, and that was 22 years ago. It’s genuinely rewarding to work closely with founders and operators across the ecosystem, witness their journey and support them through the stages of their company’s life cycle.
I recognize how rare an opportunity this is. Beauty is such a tangible industry. In terms of the average consumer, they understand beauty, but they don’t really dig deep into it, and we get that privilege of understanding all these companies from the inside out.
Being an investment banker just means that you have the real privilege of impacting everything from how an industry operates, the fate of a brand or a company, the life of a founder or entrepreneur who has started this from their kitchen, and it’s a tremendous honor to be a part of that, and something that we and I take very seriously. It’s also an incredibly fun job. It’s a challenge every day.
You never stop learning, and you never stop discovering. And it has never been boring a single day that I’ve done it. It gives me the opportunity to work with and support people at some of the most important moments of their careers and their lives, and to help them navigate that and take that to the most successful outcome.
It creates extremely deep and meaningful relationships along the way, and also gives me the opportunity to build a career and a business, and create an environment where I can support and mentor people to do the same thing, and that’s also very fulfilling. There’s just been very clear views in the past as to what a banker should look like, how a banker should talk, how a banker should act, and that’s pretty deeply embedded in the finance world.
Being aware of it and being aware of how you present yourself and what the perceptions are is just something else that comes into your career as a female investment banker. But it’s also a tremendous asset, too, because it’s an industry built around women. I started writing the musical about 17 years ago when I was an associate on a business trip, and it struck me how unique being an investment banker is.
How it’s such a different lifestyle, and I started thinking about why people make these choices. Why do people decide to devote huge amounts of their everyday life, their career, sacrifice their friendships, sacrifice their hobbies, for this job, and so my musical, which is in development, tracks the career of a young woman leaving college and entering the world of investment banking for the first time, and what that experience looks like, and how she evolves over time.
I do think that as a female, you do have to fight your way a little bit and demand your seat at the table. As a female investment banker, you can be successful in a variety of industries, but beauty and consumer in general, there is a benefit to being a female because we are the consumers, so we do have that inherent knowledge about the products.
One important thing that I feel I always need to add every time there’s a conversation around being a female and a woman banker is my goal isn’t to be the best female investment banker. My goal is to be the best investment banker. Period. What I’m striving for at any time is to deliver great outcomes for our clients.
And that’s how I try to think about the world actually. I’d also just add that mentorship with other women is extremely important, but also mentorship and relationships and advocacy from men is also extremely important. I’ve found throughout my career that sometimes we unnecessarily pigeonhole ourselves amongst women and these are the only people whose style I can replicate. These are the only people who I can turn to for advice, and that’s absolutely not the case.
I’ve had extraordinary support from many, many different folks over the course of my career, from our CEO Rich Handler on down. For someone building and navigating a career within investment banking, recognizing that while you are a woman, that isn’t and doesn’t have to be the first and most important descriptor of who you are and what you bring to the table, and there’s all sorts of people that can help you and partner with you and help you grow.
Every stage of a deal is exciting in its own way, but a few elements stand out. I particularly value the lead-up — getting to know founders, understanding their vision for the brand and seeing that come to life. It’s a privilege to be trusted with that early. During execution, every detail matters and there is real satisfaction in watching the pieces come together and helping translate a founder’s hopes and dreams into reality.
We usually go and celebrate with the company, the leadership team, our teams internally, and also just have a night where we can really talk about and reminisce on the long hours and the work that’s been done, and celebrate each other — have a few toasts to our success, and then wish people success in the next chapter. We love celebrating with the client — there’s nothing like raising a glass at a closing dinner to their success.
I equally love celebrating the team. It takes real commitment, focus and rigor to get a deal across the finish line, and it’s important to recognize everyone’s effort along the way. Right after the closing call, we do a big team call internally. We directly thank each member of our team and their contributions and what they did.
Investment banking is a team sport. There’s no single person who can make any deal happen. People are putting a lot into the deals. It’s a real sacrifice on everybody’s end.
: I’ll add the third part to that. You’ve been in the weeds for several months, if not longer. I give my kids a huge chunk of my time uninterrupted after because they probably haven’t seen me for a while. I definitely haven’t been giving them my undivided attention.
So for me, it’s also a little bit decompressing with the family if the time allows, because sometimes it does not. : It’s still very much an environment where the desire for assets is very much on a need-to-have basis versus a nice-to-have or a want-to-have, and so the bar is incredibly high. There’s a lot of interesting things happening in terms of the strategics.
For the last two-plus years, we’ve been in a world where the strategics have been rationalizing their portfolios, whether that’s through acquisitions or divestitures, and I think that’s going to keep happening. Then we’ve seen in the last 12 months or so private equity again coming to the forefront and making some big bets, and I expect that to continue as well. But the deal environment continues to shift, and it’s nothing like we’ve seen in the past.
: The word I use is metamorphosizing. Everything about the beauty industry is changing. How people shop, how they consume media, how they engage with other consumers, how they engage with brands, how they engage with products. This is probably one of the most unique times that I can remember in the last few decades, in terms of the amount of disruption in just the broader market.
So when you think about times of disruption, they’re a huge opportunity for M&A because it requires buyers and investors to shift how they’ve done things in the past and how they think about things. Meaningfully active, but extremely bifurcated. There’s still a lot of capital being put to work, but it’s definitely towards assets that are checking very specific boxes, or it’s shifting portfolios away from assets that are no longer aligned.
Then in the meantime, a lot of the private equity folks are coming in to fill in the void, or different types of buyers are participating in this space and are building their own platforms. It’s been a dynamic year with a varied complexion of transactions, from mega-mergers to portfolio pruning through corporate divestitures. That range reflects the complicated backdrop we’ve been navigating for some time now. Looking ahead, I remain optimistic.
Acquisitions have long been the growth engine for this industry, and I expect that to continue. Put yourself out there and try. Too often I see women assuming that these careers are not for them, that they don’t have the skill set, they don’t have the right training, they don’t have the right background, that finance is not a women’s sport.
We need to encourage people to step out of their comfort zone and come into the career because there’s so much opportunity for more women to explore this path, and even if banking isn’t the final stop and the final frontier, it’s a training ground that builds incredible skills. : Learn about what investment banking is before you dive into it.
You can’t go into investment banking completely blind, not knowing what to expect, because you’ll be in for a surprise. Whether that is cold outreach to analysts and associates through LinkedIn or through the alumni networks at your school, whether you’re an MBA associate or a junior or senior in college, whatever the case may be, learn as much as you can. Whether it’s banking or any other career, it’s important to just love your job.
If you love your job, you should do all the things that both Nadia and Sasha were talking about, which is really dig in, lean in, be a sponge, learn everything.
